snip.t: Three most prevalent subtypes of childhood and adolescent NHL with different treatment approaches are lymphoblastic lymphoma (LBL), mature B-cell lymphoma, and anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL.)

T/NK-cell neoplasms (10-15%): peripheral T-cell lymphoma, anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL), mycosis fungoides/Sezary syndrome, adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma (HTLV-1), NK/T-cell lymphoma (nasal type, EBV).
*Mature T/NK-cell:* Mycosis fungoides, Adult T-cell leukaemia (HTLV-1), Anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL), Peripheral T-cell lymphoma.

qs.q: Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (ALCL) is associated with which translocation and its resulting overexpressed protein?
o: t(14;18) translocation leading to BCL-2 protein overproduction
t(11;14) translocation leading to Cyclin D1 protein overproduction
t(8;14) translocation leading to MYC protein overproduction
t(2;5) translocation leading to ALK protein overproduction
qs.e: t(2;5) causes overexpression of anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). ALK+ ALCL has better prognosis than ALK− ALCL. Crizotinib specifically inhibits ALK.

es.q: Identify the characteristic chromosomal translocation and associated oncogene overexpression for TWO of the following Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma subtypes: Follicular Lymphoma, Mantle Cell Lymphoma, Burkitt Lymphoma, Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (ALCL).
es.m: 1. **Follicular Lymphoma:** Characteristic translocation is t(14;18), leading to BCL-2 overexpression. 2. **Mantle Cell Lymphoma:** Characteristic translocation is t(11;14), leading to Cyclin D1 overexpression. 3. **Burkitt Lymphoma:** Characteristic translocation is t(8;14), leading to MYC overexpression. 4. **Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (ALCL):** Characteristic translocation is t(2;5), leading to ALK overexpression. *(Candidates need to provide two correct pairs for full marks)*

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL) is a CD30‑positive T‑cell lymphoma that can present as a solitary skin nodule or systemic disease. Diagnosis relies on morphology, immunophenotype and genetic testing. Staging follows the Ann Arbor system used for other non‑Hodgkin lymphomas.

sections.p: ALCL is a mature T‑cell lymphoma characterized by large anaplastic cells that express CD30 and often ALK protein. Diagnosis requires tissue biopsy with histology, immunohistochemistry and, when available, FISH for ALK rearrangement.
b: Large pleomorphic cells with horseshoe‑shaped nuclei
Strong CD30 membranous staining
ALK‑positive (most common in children/young adults) or ALK‑negative

t.a: Excisional lymph node or skin biopsy
t.b: Does the tissue show characteristic morphology and CD30 positivity? Positive confirms lymphoma; negative prompts alternative diagnosis.
Is ALK protein expressed? Determines ALK‑positive vs ALK‑negative subtype, which influences prognosis and therapy.
Confirms ALK translocation (t(2;5)). Positive predicts better response to ALK‑targeted therapy.

sections.p: Staging uses the Ann Arbor system (I‑IV) based on number of nodal regions, extranodal involvement and systemic symptoms.
b: Stage I: single lymph node region
Stage II: two or more nodal regions on same side of diaphragm
Stage III: nodal disease on both sides of diaphragm
Stage IV: disseminated extranodal disease

t.a: CT or PET‑CT of neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis
t.b: What is the extent of nodal and extranodal disease? Determines stage and guides therapy.
Is marrow infiltrated? Positive changes stage to IV.

sections.p: ALCL is not caused by an infection but by genetic alterations, most commonly ALK translocation. In low‑resource settings, HIV infection increases risk of T‑cell lymphomas, including ALCL.
b: ALK gene rearrangement (t(2;5) NPM‑ALK) – most common in children/young adults
ALK‑negative disease – other kinase fusions (e.g., DUSP22, TP63)
Immunosuppression (HIV, post‑transplant) – raises incidence

sections.p: Patients may have a painless, rapidly enlarging lymph node or solitary skin lesion; systemic disease adds fever, night sweats, weight loss (B symptoms).
b: Solitary subcutaneous or cutaneous mass
Generalized lymphadenopathy
B symptoms in advanced disease

sections.p: Beyond histology, imaging, and laboratory work‑up are needed to assess disease burden and organ function before therapy.
b: CBC with differential – look for cytopenias
LDH level – surrogate for tumor burden
Serology for HIV in high‑risk settings

t.b: Are there anemia, thrombocytopenia, or leukopenia? May indicate marrow involvement or treatment toxicity.
Is LDH elevated? Suggests high tumor turnover and poorer prognosis.
Is patient HIV positive? Influences prognosis and may modify therapy.

sections.p: Rapid tumor growth, airway obstruction from mediastinal mass, spinal cord compression, and tumor lysis syndrome after therapy are emergencies.
b: Airway compromise from bulky mediastinal nodes
Neurologic deficits from spinal involvement
Tumor lysis syndrome after chemotherapy initiation

sections.p: First‑line therapy is multi‑agent chemotherapy (CHOP‑like regimens) combined with brentuximab vedotin for CD30‑positive disease; ALK‑positive cases may receive ALK inhibitors if refractory.
b: CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) – targets rapidly dividing cells
Brentuximab vedotin – anti‑CD30 antibody‑drug conjugate, improves outcomes
Crizotinib (ALK inhibitor) – reserved for ALK‑positive relapsed disease

sections.p: After remission, patients are monitored with periodic imaging and labs for relapse; secondary malignancies and late cardiotoxicity from anthracyclines are concerns.
b: Clinical review and CBC every 3‑6 months for 2 years
PET‑CT or CT at 6‑month intervals initially
Cardiac evaluation if anthracyclines used

sections.p: ALCL can mimic other CD30‑positive disorders and aggressive lymphomas.
b: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma – also CD30‑positive but has Reed‑Sternberg cells and different clinical pattern
Diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma – large cells but CD20‑positive, not CD30
Cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides) – slower course, different skin distribution

sections.p: Certain findings may be falsely reassuring or alarming.
b: ALK‑negative staining does not exclude ALK rearrangement if technical error occurs
Elevated LDH can be due to infection or hemolysis, not only tumor burden
PET‑CT may miss low‑grade disease despite active lymphoma

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden airway obstruction, severe dyspnea, neurological deficits, high fever with rigors, or signs of tumor lysis syndrome

faq.a: ALK‑positive ALCL generally has a better prognosis than ALK‑negative, but both are considered aggressive and need systemic therapy.

faq.q: Can ALCL arise in the skin only?
faq.a: Yes, primary cutaneous ALCL exists; it presents as solitary or few skin lesions and often has an indolent course compared with systemic disease.
CD30 is a surface marker that guides diagnosis and allows targeted therapy with brentuximab vedotin.

exam: Describe the immunophenotypic profile that distinguishes ALCL from other CD30‑positive lymphomas.
Explain how the Ann Arbor staging system is applied to ALCL and why it matters for treatment planning.
List first‑line therapeutic agents for ALCL and the rationale for adding brentuximab vedotin.
